Many people think that asking someone to repeat something makes them look weak. In fact, it is the opposite. In meetings, the people who check what they heard are usually the people who make fewer mistakes. There is a simple technique. Repeat the important part back, but change it a little. If someone says, the report is due on Friday, you say, sorry, did you say it was due on Friday? If someone says, I will call the client, you answer, great, so you said you would call the client today? The other person hears their own words, and they can correct you in one second. It takes five seconds, and it can save you a week of work.

When I started my first job in New York, I took a phone order from a client. He wanted fifteen boxes of paper. At least, that is what I heard. I was too shy to ask him to repeat it, so I wrote fifteen and said thank you. Two days later, he called again, very angry. He had asked for fifty, not fifteen, and his office had no paper for a big event. I had misheard one number, and I had not checked. Since that day, I always repeat numbers back. Did you say fifteen, one five, or fifty, five zero? It sounds a little silly, but nobody has been angry with me since then.

First, I notice that I missed something important. Then I say so politely: sorry, I didn't catch that. After that, I repeat what I think I heard: did you say it was on Friday? Next, I listen to the correction and write it down. In the end, I check the whole plan, so we're on the same page.
